deep.reconstruction:
Context: this is a draft of Riemann's Habilitationsschrift 'Ueber die Darstellbarkeit einer Function durch eine trigonometrische Reihe' (1854, published 1867). The page corresponds to the end of §5 and to §6 of the printed text: the definition of the Riemann integral and the improper integral, with illustrating examples. The previous page is the historical part on Dirichlet. The next page gives the example d(x cos e^{1/x})/dx and then begins the main investigation.

(A) Improper integrals (top of page). Suppose f may become infinite on approach to isolated points. The conditions found earlier for integrability (in the printed text: on every subinterval excluding these points, the total length of intervals where the oscillation exceeds sigma can be made arbitrarily small) remain necessary. They are no longer sufficient. In addition, the integral extended up to these points must tend to a fixed limit. Modern form: int_a^b f = lim_{eps->0} int_{a}^{c-eps} f + int_{c+eps}^{b} f. Riemann remarks that this extra condition cannot in general be stated more conveniently, and that seeking criteria for it is not useful here.

(B) First example: a function discontinuous on a dense set but integrable.
- Notation: (x) = x minus the nearest integer, with (x) = 0 when x is exactly halfway between two integers (the mean of +1/2 and -1/2). This is the marginal correction of the struck-out wording 'absolutely smallest fraction contained in x'.
- Define f(x) = sum_{n>=1} (nx)/n^2.
- Convergence (step filled in by me): |(nx)| <= 1/2, so the series is dominated by (1/2) sum 1/n^2. It therefore converges absolutely and uniformly for every x.
- Jumps: let x = p/(2n) with gcd(p, 2n) = 1, so p is odd. Then (mx) is discontinuous exactly when mx is a half-integer, i.e. m = n*q with q odd. There (mx+0) = -1/2, (mx-0) = +1/2, and (mx) = 0 at the point. Uniform convergence allows termwise limits, so:
  - f(x+0) = f(x) - (1/(2n^2)) sum_{q odd} 1/q^2 = f(x) - pi^2/(16 n^2);
  - f(x-0) = f(x) + pi^2/(16 n^2).
  At every other x, f(x+0) = f(x-0) = f(x).
- Hence f is discontinuous exactly at the rationals with even reduced denominator, with jump pi^2/(8n^2). The discontinuity is smaller the larger the denominator, and f is continuous elsewhere. 'One easily convinces oneself' that f is integrable.
- My justification of that step: for any sigma > 0, only finitely many points in [a,b] have jump > sigma. So the integrability criterion from the preceding section holds.

(C) Second topic: f infinite at a single point x = 0, assuming f is integrable (improper integral convergent).
- Claim: x f(x) cannot stay above a fixed C > 0 for all small x.
- Proof: otherwise int_x^a f dt > C int_x^a dt/t = C(log(1/x) - log(1/a)), which tends to infinity as x -> 0.
- Conclusion: if f has not infinitely many maxima and minima near 0 (so x f is eventually monotone), x f(x) must tend to 0.
- Conversely, suppose f(x) x^alpha -> 0 for some alpha < 1. Riemann writes f x^alpha = f dx (1-alpha)/d(x^{1-alpha}), since d(x^{1-alpha}) = (1-alpha) x^{-alpha} dx. Then |f| <= eps x^{-alpha}, which is integrable, so int_0 f converges.

(D) Logarithmic scale. Let L_1 = log(1/x) and L_{k+1} = log L_k (iterated logarithms; Riemann writes log^k). One has -dL_{k+1} = dx/(x L_1 ... L_k).
- Hence f x L_1 = f dx/(-dL_2), f x L_1 L_2 = f dx/(-dL_3), and generally f x L_1 ... L_{n-1} L_n = f dx/(-dL_{n+1}).
- The same comparison argument applies, because int dL_{n+1} diverges. If int_0 f converges, none of these products can stay above a positive constant as x -> 0. So, absent infinitely many maxima and minima, each must tend to 0.
- Conversely, the integral to 0 converges whenever f x L_1 ... L_{n-1} (L_n)^alpha -> 0 for some alpha > 1. Riemann writes this product as f dx (1-alpha)/(-d(L_n^{1-alpha})), and L_n^{1-alpha} -> 0 as x -> 0 when alpha > 1.
- This is the Abel/Bertrand logarithmic scale of convergence, transferred to improper integrals. It serves to illustrate the improper-integral condition of (A) before the main investigation of trigonometric series.
errors: No mathematical errors. The jump value pi^2/(16 n^2) on each side (total jump pi^2/(8n^2)) is correct.

The 'leicht zu sehen' (convergence) and 'man überzeugt sich leicht' (integrability) steps are unproved here. Both are easily supplied: the Weierstrass M-test with bound 1/(2n^2), and the fact that only finitely many jumps exceed any sigma.

The necessity statements in (C)/(D) implicitly assume f > 0 (or a fixed sign) near 0. Riemann covers this by the proviso 'if f has not infinitely many maxima and minima'. The next page addresses the oscillating case.
Slight looseness: x f > C fails 'from some bound on' only gives liminf x f <= 0. To get limit 0 one needs the monotonicity proviso, which Riemann states.

results.what: f(x) = sum (nx)/n^2: discontinuous at every rational with even denominator, jumps ±pi^2/(16n^2), yet Riemann integrable
results.modern_name: Riemann's example of an integrable function with a dense set of discontinuities

results.what: Improper integral at a singular point defined as limit of integrals extended to the point
If int_0 f converges and f is eventually monotone, then x f(x) -> 0; f x^alpha -> 0 with alpha < 1 suffices for convergence
results.modern_name: Comparison test for improper integrals with power functions

results.what: Iterated-logarithm scale: f x L1...Ln -> 0 necessary; f x L1...L_{n-1} L_n^alpha -> 0 (alpha > 1) sufficient
results.modern_name: Logarithmic (Abel–Bertrand–de Morgan) convergence scale for improper integrals
results.usually_credited_to: Abel (posthumous 1839), de Morgan, Bertrand 1842 for series; Riemann 1854 §6 for integrals

deep.surprise_reason: This is a draft of material printed almost verbatim in §6 of Riemann's 1854/1867 Habilitationsschrift. The dense-discontinuity example and the log-scale integral criteria are well known as his. The draft only offers minor wording variants, e.g. the definition of (x) via 'Ueberschuss über die nächste ganze Zahl'.

checkable.asserts: Sum of reciprocal odd squares equals pi^2/8, so (1/(2n^2))*pi^2/8 = pi^2/(16 n^2)
One-sided jump of f at x = p/(2n) is pi^2/(16 n^2); should be 0
-d log log(1/x) = dx/(x log(1/x)); should be 0 for 0<x<1
-d L3 = dx/(x L1 L2); should be 0
f x^alpha = f dx (1-alpha)/d(x^{1-alpha}); should be 0
Case n=1 of f x L1^alpha = f dx(1-alpha)/(-d L1^{1-alpha}); should be 0
int_x^a dt/t diverges (oo), giving necessity of x f -> 0

transcription_corrections: Margin insertion replaces the struck definition. Read: '(x) = den Ueberschuss von x über die nächste ganze Zahl oder, wenn x zwischen zweien gerade in der Mitte liegt, den Mittelwerth aus 1/2 und -1/2, also die Null, ferner durch n eine ganze, durch p eine ungerade Zahl'.

'welche in keinem Theile des Intervalls (ab)stetig ist' should probably be read as 'in keinem Theile ... stetig' in the sense of no subinterval free of discontinuities. In the printed text it is 'für jeden noch so kleinen Intervall unendlich oft unstetig'.
Before the logarithmic forms, the margin insertion reads 'im Fall der Convergenz des Integrals [struck: ∫fx dx] die Functionen'.
In the iterated-log formulas, log^k denotes the k-fold iterated logarithm, not a power. For n=1 the first formula is f x log(1/x) = f dx/(-d log log(1/x)), as in the image.
The second margin insertion reads roughly 'bei in's Unendliche abnehmender unteren Grenze'. The struck 'oberen/unteren Grenze' variant is uncertain.
'ist hier nicht brauchbar[?]': the reading is uncertain in the image.
